items.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: I mean you know Benny Goodman, Tommy Dorsey, Basie, Duke, they were all on what would be the rock & roll channels now. So it was great. A great experience to hear that.

ctx.x: He played full time, wow. And plus he had the radio gig.

Yeah. And then they played a lot of — oh there were places like the Kit Kat Club and the Belvedere Club and there were sort of like jazz places. And later on, after the violin episode they would take me to hear the band rehearse and things. So actually it was a very fruitful time for music because the pop stations were playing all the heavy bands. I mean you know Benny Goodman, Tommy Dorsey, Basie, Duke, they were all on what would be the rock & roll channels now. So it was great. A great experience to hear that.
That was the popular music. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

items.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: Because both Dorseys were alive then.

ctx.x: Yeah. I guess I had this fairly misconstrued idea that the big bands almost like disappeared in the latter 40s. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

No I think they – they weren’t as hot as they were. But I think the big bands didn’t — well I think they were really almost over at the end of the 50s. Because both Dorseys were alive then. Benny was still alive then. Even the bands like Henry Busse and bands that people really didn’t want to go out with but they would to get road experience. But when I was on Maynard’s band in the 60s, the first half of the 60s, we used to play dances and there was standing room only. And there were a lot of kids too, which was…
Yes. Did the prospect of the draft frighten you?
